response.title: If I buy a 3D scanner for car parts, what software turns the scan into something I can edit in CAD without paying thousands a year?
response.answer:
You do not need to spend thousands per year to turn 3D scans of car parts into editable CAD models. There are several free and affordable options.

The important distinction is between editing a scanned mesh and turning that mesh into real parametric CAD geometry.

For automotive work—brackets, intake manifolds, suspension components, body panels, custom mounts—the second is usually what you want.

1. The software I'd consider

Software

	

Cost

	

Best use




FreeCAD

	

Free, open source

	

Rebuilding mechanical parts as editable parametric CAD




Autodesk Fusion

	

Free personal tier with restrictions; paid tiers

	

Designing new parts using scans as references




Blender

	

Free

	

Cleaning scans, editing meshes, bodywork and organic shapes




MeshLab

	

Free

	

Cleaning, simplifying and repairing raw scan meshes




CloudCompare

	

Free

	

Aligning scans, comparing surfaces and checking dimensions




Rhino 3D

	

One-time license

	

Surface modeling for body panels and complex automotive shapes

My starting recommendation: FreeCAD + Blender + CloudCompare. You can build a useful reverse-engineering workflow without recurring software fees.

2. The catch: converting a scan to CAD isn't automatic

Typical workflow

3D scan

Capture

STL / OBJ mesh

Clean

Rebuild geometry

Model

Editable STEP / CAD

Manufacture

A scanner typically gives you millions of triangles. CAD software can convert those triangles into a solid, but that doesn't automatically recreate cylinders, holes, sketches, fillets, and dimensions.

For example, scanning a mounting bracket and converting it to a solid might give you 50,000 tiny faces rather than six clean surfaces and four editable holes.

FreeCAD supports mesh-to-shape conversion, but proper parametric reconstruction is a separate task. 
GitHub
+1

3. What I'd use for different car parts

Brackets, mounts, spacers, adapters

Use FreeCAD. Recreate holes, planes, and dimensions from the scan. There's also a newer experimental MeshToFeatures add-on that attempts to reconstruct editable features automatically, although noisy real-world scans remain a limitation. 
GitHub
+1

Intake manifolds, castings, complex housings

Use Blender + FreeCAD. Clean the scan in Blender, then reconstruct functional surfaces in FreeCAD. Expect some manual work.

Fenders, bumpers, dashboards, body panels

Use Rhino 8 for complex surface reconstruction. It has QuadRemesh and SubD tools and currently costs about $995 once, with no mandatory annual maintenance fee. 
Buy
+1

4. One paid option worth considering

Rhino 8 is particularly interesting if you're modifying car body panels or building custom aerodynamic parts. Unlike many engineering CAD packages, it offers a perpetual license.

Fusion is also capable, but its free personal license is restricted to noncommercial use, and converting dense scan meshes can create performance problems. 
Autodesk
+1

5. One question that changes my recommendation

What kinds of car parts are you primarily planning to scan?

Mechanical parts — brackets, mounts, suspension, adapters
Engine parts — intake manifolds, engine bays, castings
Bodywork — bumpers, fenders, spoilers, dashboards
A mix of everything
Recommend my workflow

That determines whether you can get away with entirely free software or whether a one-time purchase would save you substantial modeling time.
